newsitem.title: UK: Analysts raise forecasted 1997 copper prices - poll.
newsitem.headline: Analysts raise forecasted 1997 copper prices - poll.

text.p: Unexpected supply tightness in the first part of the year has forced market analysts to raise their forecasts for average copper prices in 1997, according to a Reuters survey published on Monday.

The tighter supply/demand balance has helped drive London Metal Exchange (LME) prices to the highest in nearly a year, with three months prices nearing $2,500 per tonne, compared to $2,130 in January.
Prices were last trading at $2,470 Monday morning.

Surging Western demand, combined with the end of a prolonged period of de-stocking and continuing robust growth in the developing world have boosted most of the base metals, said analyst Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff.
Copper in particular is going to benefit in the first part of the year from supply hiccups and labour problems cropping up in Chile and elsewhere, he said.

"Copper is expected to remain tight and vulnerable to further price spikes, because of ongoing start up problems such as at the Garfield smelter in North America, and industrial disputes at various smelters and mines, in particular in South America," Squires said.

Despite demand being firmer than expected and supply tighter in the first half of 1997, several of the nine analysts surveyed highlighted that they still expected copper to go into surplus this year as new production capacity comes on stream.
But the timing of the expected flood of new material is still an unknown quantity, brokers Billiton said in a report earlier this month.
"Few disagree that there is a huge volume of metal headed for the market," said Billiton, which forecasts a substantial surplus this year and next but nevertheless revised its copper forecast higher.

"The difference of opinion revolves around the speed at which this will occur and the extent to which this metal will be absorbed by a combination of Western demand and Chinese offtake," the report added.
Forecasts for the other base metals were also tweaked from levels set in a similar poll in January, but less so than copper.
Zinc performed better than expected in the first part of the year and already bullish forecasts were adjusted somewhat higher.
Aluminium forecasts were little changed, and analysts noted that robust demand would continue carrying the market higher throughout the year.
But nickel, tin and lead prices were revised slightly lower by some analysts as these markets underperformed expectations.
